title: Stunning Sacrifice: Close the King’s Last Escape
summary: Offer the queen to block the king’s escape, then distinguish a checking pawn push from the final pawn recapture that actually mates.

nodes.question: How can Black force mate despite being a rook down?
nodes.explanation: Qe4+ offers the queen on a square that White must occupy. Pawn checks then close the king’s escape routes; the h4 pawn still gets a checking capture before Black’s f-pawn delivers mate.

branches.title: Source line: the bishop takes the queen
commentary: Begin with the complete sixteen-piece board. Black must create a forcing attack before White’s extra rook matters.
Qe4+ offers the queen with check on e4, not d4. White has only Bxe4 or Kxe4; moving another piece or simply retreating the king cannot answer the check legally.
Bxe4 accepts the queen, placing White’s own bishop on the e4 escape square.
e5+ checks Kf4 with the pawn from e6. The bishop on e4 and Black’s other controls leave only one legal reply.
dxe5 takes the checking pawn, but White’s own pawn now occupies e5 and blocks another potential king flight.
g5+ checks Kf4 with the g7 pawn advancing two squares. This is not mate: the h4 pawn can capture it with check.
hxg5+ is White’s only legal reply. It removes the checking pawn and checks Kh6 from g5, so Black must still answer that check.
fxg5# takes the white pawn with the pawn from f6 and checks Kf4. White’s bishop and e5 pawn block e4/e5; Bg4 and Black’s pawns cover the other flights. White has no legal reply: actual mate.
branches.explanation: fxg5# takes the white pawn with the pawn from f6 and checks Kf4. White’s bishop and e5 pawn block e4/e5; Bg4 and Black’s pawns cover the other flights. White has no legal reply: actual mate.

branches.title: Source alternative: the king takes the queen
commentary: Compare White’s only other reply to the same queen offer. Both branches are illustrated source variations, not a full historical game score.
Qe4+ forces White to take the queen with king or bishop.
Kxe4 uses the king and leaves Bd3 on its original square. Black needs an extra pawn check to restore Kf4.
d5+ advances the d7 pawn two squares, checking the king on e4.
Kf4 is forced back. White still has its queen, rook and bishop, but none can interrupt the coming close-range pawn checks.
e5+ forces the d4 pawn to capture, recreating the self-blockade on e5.
dxe5 removes the checking pawn and fills the e5 escape square with White’s own pawn.
g5+ checks the king. As in the other branch, hxg5+ remains legal and must not be omitted from the calculation.
hxg5+ answers the pawn check with a checking capture against Kh6. White’s h-pawn is now on g5 rather than h4.
fxg5# answers that check and delivers actual mate. Black’s d5 pawn also controls e4, filling the role played by White’s bishop in the other variation.

exercises.prompt: Why give the queen away on e4?
exercises.answer: White must take with bishop or king. The bishop blocks e4 directly; if the king takes, d5+ forces it back to f4 and also controls e4.
No. White’s h4 pawn can play hxg5+, checking Kh6. Black then plays f6xg5#, which answers the check and actually mates.

sourceCorrections.claim: The caption names the queen offer as d4.
sourceCorrections.correction: The board shows Qe4+, which is legal and forces Bxe4 or Kxe4.

sourceCorrections.claim: The narrated g5 push is described as pawn checkmate.
sourceCorrections.correction: g5+ allows the forced hxg5+. The later source image confirms fxg5#, the actual mate. The earlier review correctly found hxg5+ but stopped before this visually supported recapture.
